::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### What a data acquisition system does to a voltage {#sec-s1-chain}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### What a data acquisition system does to a voltage (1)
:::

Between the quantity you care about and the number in your file there is a
chain, and every link adds something of its own. For S1 the chain is short on
purpose — a voltage straight into an analog input — so that what we measure is
the acquisition system itself and nothing else.

$$
\underbrace{V}_{\text{measurand}}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\underbrace{(1 + \varepsilon_G)\,V + V_{os} + \mathrm{INL}(V)}_{\text{static errors}}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\underbrace{+\,\eta}_{\text{noise}}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\underbrace{\mathrm{round}(\cdot/q)}_{\text{quantization}}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\underbrace{N}_{\text{code}}
$$ {#eq-s1-chain}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### What a data acquisition system does to a voltage (2)
:::

The four terms are different in kind, and the whole experiment is about
telling them apart:

- $\varepsilon_G$, the **gain error**, and $V_{os}$, the **offset**, are
  systematic and *correctable*. You measure them once and subtract them
  afterwards; what remains in the budget is the uncertainty of the correction,
  not the error itself.
- $\mathrm{INL}(V)$, the **integral nonlinearity**, is systematic but not
  described by two numbers. Unless you characterize it point by point it
  remains as a bound: an interval you cannot correct within.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### What a data acquisition system does to a voltage (3)
:::

- $\eta$, the **noise**, is random. It averages down as $1/\sqrt{N}$, which is
  why it is the one term you can trade measurement time against.
- **Quantization** is deterministic given the input, but over a population of
  inputs it behaves like a bounded random error, and that is how the GUM
  treats it.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Quantization {#sec-s1-quantization}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Quantization (1)
:::

The converter reports an integer code $N$. The driver turns it back into volts
with full scale $2^n - 1$:

$$
V_\mathrm{ind} = N\,q, \qquad q = \frac{V_\mathrm{ref}}{2^{n} - 1}
$$ {#eq-s1-lsb}

$q$ is one **LSB**. Any voltage within $\pm q/2$ of a code produces that code,
so the code tells you the voltage only to within that interval. Knowing
nothing else, the GUM assigns a rectangular distribution of half-width $q/2$,
whose standard deviation is

$$
u_q = \frac{q}{\sqrt{12}}
$$ {#eq-s1-uq}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The $\sqrt{12}$ is not a convention, it is the standard deviation of a uniform
distribution on an interval of width $q$: $\int_{-q/2}^{q/2} x^2\,\mathrm{d}x/q
= q^2/12$. It appears again in @eq-s1-enob and again, with $q = 1\,\mu$s, for
the timestamps in @sec-s1-timing. Whenever you know a bound and nothing about
what happens inside it, this is the number you use.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Quantization (2)
:::

On a board reporting $n = 16$ bits with $V_\mathrm{ref} = 3.3$ V,
$q \approx 50.4\ \mu$V and $u_q \approx 14.5\ \mu$V. Hold on to those figures:
by the end of the experiment you will find that they are the *smallest* term
in the budget by a wide margin, and that is the first real result.

### Noise, and how many bits are actually there {#sec-s1-enob}

Feed the converter a constant voltage and read it many times. If the only
imperfection were quantization you would get one code, or two adjacent codes
if the input sat near a transition. What you actually get is a distribution
several codes wide: the input stage, the reference and the converter itself
all contribute noise, and the result is that the last few bits of the reading
carry no information.

The usual way to say how many bits are left is to ask what resolution an
*ideal* converter would need to produce the observed spread. An ideal $m$-bit
converter over a full-scale range FSR has quantization noise
$\mathrm{FSR}/(2^m\sqrt{12})$; setting that equal to the measured standard
deviation $\sigma$ gives the **effective number of bits**

$$
\mathrm{ENOB} = \log_2\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{FSR}}{\sqrt{12}\,\sigma}\right)
$$ {#eq-s1-enob}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Two warnings about @eq-s1-enob. First, it is the *static* effective resolution:
it describes a converter fed a constant, and it says nothing about what happens
at 10 kHz, where aperture jitter and settling matter. The dynamic ENOB of IEEE
Std 1241 [@ieee1241], measured from the residuals of a fitted sine, is a
different and generally smaller number; S2 measures it and the two should be
compared. Second, manufacturers often quote *noise-free* resolution instead,

$$
\mathrm{ENOB}_\mathrm{nf} = \log_2\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{FSR}}{6.6\,\sigma}\right)
$$ {#eq-s1-enob-nf}

using a $\pm 3.3\sigma$ peak-to-peak span, which is about $0.9$ bits fewer.
Neither is wrong; quoting one and calling it the other is.
:::

### Averaging, and what it cannot fix {#sec-s1-averaging}

The mean of $N$ independent readings has standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt{N}$.
Take 200 readings and the random part of your reading improves by a factor of
14. Take 20 000 and it improves by 141.

What does not improve at all is $V_{os}$, $\varepsilon_G$ and
$\mathrm{INL}(V)$. They are the same on every reading, so the mean converges
to the *wrong* value with beautiful precision. This is the single most
important practical lesson of S1, and the uncertainty budget at the end makes
it arithmetic rather than rhetoric: once $N$ is a few hundred, the Type A term
drops below the calibration terms and buying more time buys nothing.

### Calibrating offset and gain {#sec-s1-calibration}

Apply $k$ known voltages $V_i$, each measured with a reference instrument, and
record the mean indication $\bar{V}_{\mathrm{ind},i}$ at each. Fit

$$
\bar{V}_\mathrm{ind} = a + b\,V
$$ {#eq-s1-fit}

so that $a$ estimates the offset and $b - 1$ the gain error. The corrected
reading of an unknown is then

$$
\hat{V} = \frac{V_\mathrm{ind} - a}{b}
$$ {#eq-s1-correct}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Three points is the minimum that gives you a residual at all, and a tier-1
bench can produce exactly three: a shorted input, a voltage reference IC, and
the reference through a resistive divider. With three points you get one degree
of freedom for the residual, which is enough to notice nonlinearity but not
enough to characterize it — so it enters the budget as a bound, from the
largest residual, rather than as a correction.

The uncertainties of $a$ and $b$ come from the fit, and they are correlated.
Ignoring that correlation is a simplification this experiment makes
deliberately and states in the budget; @eq-s1-correct with independent $a$ and
$b$ overestimates the uncertainty at the ends of the range and underestimates
it in the middle. A full treatment propagates the covariance matrix of the fit,
which is the natural extension for a postgraduate group.
:::

The sensitivity coefficients of @eq-s1-correct, needed for the budget, are

$$
\frac{\partial \hat V}{\partial V_\mathrm{ind}} = \frac{1}{b},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat V}{\partial a} = -\frac{1}{b},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat V}{\partial b} = -\frac{V_\mathrm{ind} - a}{b^{2}}
$$ {#eq-s1-sensitivity}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Timestamps: is the sampling grid real? {#sec-s1-timing}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Timestamps: is the sampling grid real? (1)
:::

Every streamed record carries the device's own `micros()` value. Sampling runs
from `loop()`, not from a timer interrupt, so the grid is *requested*, not
guaranteed, and part of S1 is finding out what was actually delivered.

Fit the timestamps against their index by least squares,

$$
\hat{t}_i = \hat{t}_0 + i\,\hat{T},
\qquad
r_i = t_i - \left(\hat{t}_0 + i\,\hat{T}\right)
$$ {#eq-s1-grid}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Timestamps: is the sampling grid real? (2) {.smaller}
:::

and read the residuals. There are three signatures, and they mean different
things:

| Residual pattern | Mechanism | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Flat band, no trend | Bounded jitter: the record lands on the first `loop()` iteration after its due time | Adds noise to any time-derivative; harmless for static work |
| Straight slope | $\hat{T}$ is not the true period — a clock or rate error | Frequencies are all wrong by the same factor; correctable |
| Steps | Schedule restart after a late record | The grid is piecewise; a periodogram over the whole record is meaningless |

: Reading the residuals of @eq-s1-grid {#tbl-s1-residuals}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The step case deserves attention because the firmware chooses it deliberately.
When a record is late, the device restarts its schedule from that moment
instead of emitting a burst of catch-up records. That is the right decision —
catch-up records would carry timestamps that are lies — but it means a hiccup
appears as one long interval and a permanent shift of everything after it.
Detecting the long intervals and either splitting the record or discarding it
is part of the analysis, not an optional refinement.

Since `t_us` is an integer, every timestamp carries $u_q = 1\,\mu\mathrm{s}/\sqrt{12}
\approx 0.29\ \mu$s of quantization uncertainty from @eq-s1-uq. At 1 kHz that
is $3 \times 10^{-4}$ of the period and you may ignore it; at 30 kHz it is
about 1 % and you may not.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Two influence quantities you cannot see in the data {#sec-s1-influence}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Two influence quantities you cannot see in the data (1)
:::

An **influence quantity** is something that affects the result without being
the measurand. S1 has two worth naming.

**Inter-channel skew.** When several pins are streamed, the firmware reads them
in one pass of `loop()` — sequentially — and gives every sample in the record
*the same* timestamp. The samples are therefore not simultaneous, and the
difference is one conversion time per channel of separation. For a constant
input this changes nothing. For a signal changing at $\dot{V}$ it is a
systematic error of $\dot{V}\,\Delta t$ on the later channel, and it is
invisible in the file, because the timestamps claim simultaneity.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Two influence quantities you cannot see in the data (2)
:::

**The host operating system.** The board samples on its own, but the host has
to drain the bulk endpoint. A host that is late makes the device's buffer
overrun and the schedule restart. Nothing about the board changed; the numbers
in your file did. This is why every sidecar records the host, and why S1 ends
by acquiring the same signal twice on two different hosts and comparing the
timing statistics — the honest way to establish which host your later
experiments should run on.
